item.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search for Kernel Generation
item.description:
Important Links

Luigi’s source repo

List of optimization strategies

List of performance states

Notes on applying AlphaGo Zero’s approach to Kernel Generation

AlphaGo Zero Paper

Spec file

The Spec file describes decision in much more detail. This blog entry is a high-level summary.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a test-time compute strategy to find an optimal action.

In two-player games, the state is the current board, actions are possible moves (i.e. legal moves) and the goal is to find the action that maximizes the probability of winning. The moves are deterministic. One does a full MCTS search (will be described in more detail but treat it as a black-box for now) for each move since the next move is made by the opponent. MCTS generates an asymmetric tree where each node is a board state, and each edge is a legal move that points the tail state (before the move) to the head state (after the move).

GPU kernel generation is a single-player game. MCTS is carried out for each workload section 5 consisting of:

  • Operation e.g. matrix multiplication

  • Hardware e.g. H100 SXM

  • dtype e.g. NVFP4

  • Tensor shape constraints e.g. each dimension in .

The spec also includes other factors like:

  • Tensor layouts e.g. row-major contiguous matrices, column-major, strided batched tensors, interleaved QKV layouts, packed low-precision formats etc.

  • Numerical tolerances e.g. absolute (atol=) and relative (rtol=) for a given format e.g. FP32.

  • Kernel launch parameters e.g. block and grid sizes, shared memory bytes.

  • Distribution over shapes for dataset e.g. . Note the reward will be an expectation over this distribution.

The list might expand over time.

Nodes

Each node (section 7) is a specific GPU kernel version for the chosen workload. The initial focus is on CUDA C++. General interfaces defining backends can be extended to CuTeDSL and CUTLASS.

Section 7 also declares a set of variables to be stored for each node. A subset is:

  • program_text: source code

  • backend_type: CUDA C++, CuTeDSL, CUTLASS

  • normalized_program_hash and binary_has_or_sass_hash: hashes of both the source code and generated SASS code. Hashes let us refer to previously computed results instead of re-evaluating performance of an already generated kernel. For more details, see section 21.

  • benchmark_results: performance results from running the node kernel version.

  • reward: numerical record of i.e. average reward achieved when passing through this node.

  • lightweight_profile and full_profile: statistics from running ncu.

  • children/action statistics: priors, number of calls to each action etc.

  • created_by_strategy: record which action/strategy led to this node from its parent

  • created_by_llm_generation_id: log info about LLM session which consisted of parent node’s kernel code, strategy prompt and profile metrics which led to current node’s kernel.

Edges

An edge is a strategy/action. These prompts are stored in a config file for each backend (CUDA C++, CuTeDSL, CUTLASS).

At a given node, the action with the maximum score is chosen (section 9) where

This strategy is known as PUCT (Polynomial Upper Confidence Trees).

Technical point: this defines the tree policy during the Expansion phase in MCTS. We don’t use rollouts here (neither does AlphaGo Zero; see section 15). At lead nodes, we profile and evaluate. AlphaGo Zero uses the value estimator at a leaf node instead of rolling out.

The first-term in the score is a direct measure of the average reward achieved when one passes through this node. In other words, all the trajectories of applying optimizations that took action in the state will eventually achieve some reward (log speedup) and the average value of the rewards is the first term.

The second-term encourages exploration even when the reward is low for a node. is a hyperparameter that weights the relative terms. is a prior probability assigned to each action for a given state . This could be fixed by us (e.g. uniform prior) or generated by an LLM. is the number of times action was taken in state . The term $ effectively encourages taking an action that has a low visitation count relative to the total number of visitations to the state .

Stochasticity

In a deterministic environment e.g. Go or Chess, taking an action (move) in a state (board) always results in the same final state (new board). If the same node/state is revisited, and a previously taken action is retaken, we can reuse past information.

LLMs are stochastic. At each step i.e. for each new token generation, the distribution generated by the last layer softmax is sampled which results in stochasticity.

The takeaway is that applying the same action to the same kernel source will result in different code generation for the child node.

Technical point: If the profiling is done again, there’ll also be stochasticity in ncu metrics.

Sections 10, 11, 12 describe how we treat this stochastic behavior.

Section 10 shows what the tree looks like:

INSERT IMAGE

Each current-node can have several children for a given strategy (unlike in determinstic settings where there is exactly one child per chosen action).

Section 11 describes a heuristic called progressive widening. This decides how many candidates to generate for a given strategy at a node. The general bound is:

where = number of children at node/state s and for action/strategy a, is a constant hyperparameter (default=1.0), is the total number of times action/strategy a was taken at node/state s and lastly, is a hyperparameter (default=0.5).

Our default choice is:

with a hard constraint that can never exceed a hyperparameter, or more succinctly,

By default, .

Section 12 describes exactly how progressive widening takes place. At a given node s, when an action a is taken (by using PUCT described above), we have two cases:

Case A: Allow a new child

Generate a new candidate from the LLM.

Case B: Don’t allow a new child

Support, progressive widening doesn’t allow more children. Then, we need to pick an existing child. We will simply use UCB but should explore different strategies in later iterations. UCB is described in more detail next.

Suppose, the state s with action a has 4 children:

Since we can’t generate more children, we need a score to pick one child. UCB defines score:

where is the average reward when one passes through , is a scalar hyperparameter, is the number of times action a was called in state s, is the number of times action a was called in state s and child was picked.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning Reading Group #3 - Deep Q-learning (DQN)
item.description:
This article covers implementation notes for Deep Q-learning (DQN) on Atari as described in the original nature paper. The goal is to write down the distinct components and design choices before we write any code. Ideally, writing the code for DQN should be a purely mechanical activity although realistically, a few choices are made much clearer during implementation e.g. code optimizations and some design choices.

Recall that satisfies the Bellman equation:

(including in the expectation for environments with stochastic rewards).

Note that we can take the expectation over “into” the linear sum i.e.

The optimal Q-value function satisfies:

We want to learn the optimal . This quantity lets us pick optimal actions in any state by picking the action that maximizes . In other words, knowing defines a deterministic policy by (as long as no two actions have exactly the same value for a given state). Note that the “max” is also an expectation under a deterministic policy. This can be seen as follows - the definition of expectation is:

Under a deterministic policy, one has probability 1 while the rest have probabilities 0 i.e.

For , this action is precisely the one that maximizes which results in the Bellman optimality equation consisting of the .

These Bellman equations are constraints i.e. they require consistency between evaluated for various (s,a) pairs. There is one constraint/equation/consistency condition for each pair. We saw this explicitly in the tabular Q-learning example. Estimating for each pair doesn’t scale well as state-space and action-space sizes increase.

One can instead use a function approximator i.e. a model that approximates the function:

where are the model’s weights if one uses a linear model or a neural network.

In practice, the neural network takes the state (stacked image frames for Atari) as inputs and produces (number of actions) Q-values as outputs.

Of course, we first need to train the neural network using some supervised objective i.e. by minimizing a loss of the form:

i.e. a mean squared loss error with some target value averaged over the distribution of state-action pairs seen in the data (replay buffer).

The Bellman equation tells us exactly what the target should be:

The expectation is approximated by a single sample(!) as:

Note: In taking a single sample, we introduce higher variance into the computation. As shown below (point 2), since we don’t know , we use a noisy estimate, . The max chooses the that maximizes this estimate which preferentially chooses actions that had a positive noise fluctuation. This will motivate Double DQN.

Computing requires two components:

  1. Tuples where label the state-action pair for which the constraint is being applied. is the new state transitioned into for the single sample chosen to approximate the expectation value. is the observed reward since we usually don’t know the reward function and can’t compute but can observe this value.

  2. The target also needs . But this is the quantity the neural network is trying to approximate. So the loss looks like where both the predicted value and the target depend on . While we’ll explore this more quantitatively, this leads to unstable training since it’s equivalent to supervised learning where the prediction and the label can both be changed by gradient descent. Instead, like in the tabular case, we use an iterative approach.

The standard solution to (2) is to use the iterative nature of updates to . If the current model is , the target is computed using a lagged model i.e. with a smaller . For example, we might use the model every 10th iteration to compute the target. So, iterations to would use to compute the target. Iterations to would use to compute targets and so on. The target equation for iteration updates to:

To summarize, we will approximate the Q-function with a neural network that predicts the optimal action-value for all actions in one forward pass i.e. there is one output per action for . The network is trained using the Bellman optimality condition to define a target. The target also requires values and to avoid training instabilities, we use a lagged version of to compute the target. The simplest choice for the state can be the current image frame (RGB or grayscale). To inject information about velocity and acceleration, we can stack consecutive frames.

As noted earlier, each loss term depends on one tuple. Each trajectory e.g. one instance of a game produces consecutive tuples

which can be decomposed into tuples:

These tuples are highly correlated which reduces the effective amount of information being collected. To break this correlation, one accumulates tuples from various trajectories into a buffer (the replay or experience replay buffer) of fixed size . A batch of tuples is then sampled randomly which ensures that tuples from different trajectories are trained over in each batch.

A subtle point: we are not approximating . If we were, we would be on-policy i.e. we would need to collect tuples under the policy , train to approximate , improve the policy and then collect more tuples.

We are instead learning . This is independent of the data collection policy! It is by definition at least as good as any i.e.

To learn , it doesn’t matter what policy the data is collected under and we can mix various data collection policies together i.e. we can have a buffer/array of tuples collected under different policies.

Fine-print 1: The data collection policies are relevant for coverage. If a pair is never visited, we can’t compute . But as long as we keep visiting under any policy, we have some data that can be used to infer .

Fine-print 2: For tabular Q-learning, fine-print 1 applies. For function approximation (e.g. using an NN to approximate , not only does fine-print 1 apply but the distribution of tuples is important during training because SGD will tradeoff approximation errors in seen data (reflected by the loss) with approximation errors in unseen data. More precisely, (a) there are no guarantees on unseen data - the approximation error might be large or small, and (b) even in seen tuples, under-represented tuples might have larger errors than well-represented tuples.

In general, the combination of function approximation (neural net in our case), bootstrapping (using to define the target), and off-policy learning (buffer of tuples collected under different policies) can actually cause learning to become unstable where in theory. In practice, these values can grow to unrealistic values but can also recover. This is known as the deadly triad. Small errors can compound rapidly e.g. see paper.

Implementation Notes

Initial Environment

Do all initial experiments with Pong. This is especially helpful for debugging.

A good candidate for the next game is Breakout (see famous story about Woz and Jobs at Atari).

Run multiple seeds - at least 3-5 per experiment.

Use Gymnasium. ale-py has the games.

Hardware

NVIDIA 3090/4090 should be enough since env is CPU-bound. Ensure you have enough vCPUs available.

Ablations

The following is a non-exhaustive list of ablations:

Replay Buffer Size: As stated above, the replay buffer breaks correlations between tuples. Tuples are added to the buffer and old ones are evicted to ensure the buffer doesn’t exceed a maximum size. As the buffer is made smaller, we approach a more online sampling procedure where all tuples are from recent episodes and are therefore, more correlated.

Vary the buffer size e.g. 1, 100, 10000, 1M and observe the learning curves.

Frame Stacking: For various games, change the stacking size e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8 etc. to observe the impact including higher-derivative information (velocity, acceleration etc.)

Target Network Freezing: Use the current network to calculate the target. A more comprehensive experiment would change the freezing frequency from 1 (no freezing) to 10k (paper’s value) to a much higher value.

: To encourage exploration, a parameter is introduced. Usually it’s chosen to be small e.g. . With probability , a completely random action is chosen and with probability , the action chosen is .

During training, is annealed from high (e.g. 1.0 i.e. fully random policy) values to low (e.g. ) values with a linearly decaying schedule.

During evaluation, is fixed to small values (0.05) to avoid getting stuck in loops.

Can try various decay schedules and also try keeping .

item.title: Reinforcement Learning Reading Group #2 - Prerequisites
item.description:
IN PROGRESS

In the last entry, we covered the basic formalism of a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We looked at state and action spaces, rewards, trajectories and policies.

In this write-up, we’ll look at two crucial quantities. Suppose, we are given the following:

  • An environment i.e. a state space , an action space and a simulator (or real-life setup) that can execute the unknown (to us) transition function .

  • A reward function which can be used to compute trajectory level rewards where is the discount factor (in ).

  • A policy that takes a state as an input and maps to an action. The policy can be determinstic (map state to one action) or stochastic (for a given state, produce a probability for picking each action).

The central task in RL is to pick a good policy. Recall that a policy is a rule that maps states to actions i.e.  (determinstic policy) or states to probabilities over actions if there are N distinct actions. In short, policies tell an actor (also known as the agent) how to act or what decisions to make. Intuitively, a “good” policy will lead to trajectories that have “high” rewards, .

To identify high-reward actions, it’s useful to compute two quantities:

  • The “quality” score of a state . This quantity assesses if it’s desirable to land up in this state. Formally, this is called the state value function . For convenience, is also referred to as the value function.

  • The “quality” score of an action in a given state. This quantity assesses how desirable it is to take an action in the given state. Formally, this is called the state-action value function . For convenience, is also called the Q-function or Q-value.

Let’s define the two quantities.

State-action value function

Assume we’re given a policy , which lets us generate trajectories.

Suppose, at time t in a trajectory, we land in state and are forced to take an action . The transition function will take into a state according to the probability . We can now use the policy to generate the next action, land in a new state according to the transition function and so on till some stopping criterion is satisfied. At each step, we’ll get a reward and we can define a partial-trajectory reward known as reward to-go:

It might be helpful to set to see that is simply the some of future rewards (“to-go”) starting from time . The notation is used to be consistent with Sutton and Barto’s book in case you use it although they start the sum at (different definition).

To summarize, given a state at time and a forced action at time t, we can rollout the trajectory with policy and compute a number that’s the reward to-go.

If we were to repeat this experiment, we would get a different trajectory after time . This is because:

  • The policy might be stochastic and not determinstic i.e.  gives a distribution over actions ( with probability 40%, with probability 60%) and repeated runs will choose different actions (see aside on sampling below).

  • The transition function might be stochastic and not determinstic i.e. even if one takes the same action in the same state, defines a probability distribution over and we’ll end up in different states in repeated runs.

Aside on sampling:

Suppose, we have three possible actions:

with probability 0.4

with probability 0.5

with probability 0.1

We could just choose since it has the highest probability. Another option is to sample i.e. pick different actions according to their probabilities, as shown i figure 1 below.

Since all the probabilities have to add up to 1, put them consecutively on the interval. Sample a uniform random number and place it on the interval. In the figure, is drawn and placed. It lands in the interval “owned” by and so we would pick . In general the probability of a random number landing in one of the intervals is proportional to the length of the interval.

End of Aside

For each sub-trajectory starting at with action , we have one reward to-go value, . We can now define the “quality” of (, ) as the average (over all trajectories generated beyond time ) .

This is written more formally as:

We’ll unpack this shortly. Intuitively, you should think of as the “average discounted cumulative reward (reward to-go) if one is forced to take action in state and then take future actions according to the policy ”. The part of using the policy to take future actions is crucial and is made explicit by writing .

Let’s now unpack:

The first important piece is . This is called the expected value. More precisely, in probability theory, one works with objects called random variables. You can think of a random variable as a quantity take can take multiple values, each with a specific probability. The simplest example or a random variable is a coin toss i.e.

The expected value of X i.e.  is the average outcome i.e.

This might look mysterious so let’s look at an illustrative example. Suppose you are given the following data for test scores for 10 students:

The average score would be:

The ratios are precisely the probabilities of picking students with certain scores i.e. the % of students with each unique score:

In other words, the average is the “sum of each unique value multiplied by the probability of observing the value”. Mathematically, we could write:

where the sum is over all unique values can take. Often the probability distribution is made explicit by writing .

Going back to :

We see that the random variable is . The part signifies that we have a known fixed state and known fixed action at time . Lastly, specifies that actions are sampled from the transition function and actions are sampled from the policy .

Theoretically, you could think of computing as follows:

  • Generate every possible trajectory start at time by taking actions from policy and letting states evolve according to the transition function .

  • Select the subset of trajectories that hit state at time and where the action taken is at time .

  • For the subset of trajectories, compute the discounted reward to-go for every trajectory.

  • Average these reward to-go values to get .

This is computationally intractable. For example, if we have distinct states and distinct actions, and each trajectory has time-steps, we have a total of trajectories. Even for small values of e.g. , this is i.e. 100 billion billion. If it takes one second to do one rollout, it would take years to generate every trajectory sequentially. This is a trillion years (the universe is about 14 billion years old).

We now understand how to evaluate the quality of a state-action pair using . Mathematically (and programmatically), is a function that maps a state-action pair to a number.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning Reading Group #1 - Prerequisites
item.description:
This is hopefully the first of a series of write-ups for a group of engineers ramping up on RL. We will be reading papers and implementing a subset from the Spinning up RL list.

There is no shortage of great resources on RL but the goal here is to write the simplest description of concepts and code for our group.

Formal Setup for RL

The central question is how to make a sequence of decisions in a given circumstance. The rest of this write-up makes this question more formal.

We need to define the following:

  • What do mean by “a given circumstance”? As an example, think of driving a car as the circumstance or task.

  • What is a decision? In the example, “braking”, “steering left by 10 degrees”, “steering right by 10 degrees”, “accelerator at 50%” could be some decisions.

  • How frequently do decision need to be made? One decision every 1 second would be too infrequent since a car at 60mph (~100kph) travels ~28m (~90 feet) in that time.

  • Given a sequence of already picked decisions, how do we evaluate the quality of the sequence? Alternately, what makes us prefer one sequence of decisions over another sequence?

The rest of this write-up answers and formalizes the questions above. This formalization provides the basic framework for all the RL papers we’ll read.

Decisions or Actions

The easiest object to define is the decision-space (generally known as the action-space), , which is simply the set of all possible decisions/actions that can be executed.

States

To make a decision, one first needs some input information. In the car driving example, we make decisions based on what we see and possibly what we hear, on latent/hidden information about our purpose for driving (“going to the local park”) and on latent/hidden information about our mood (driving rashly when angry or driving slow when on a leisure drive). One can add more features like the state of the car. If the front-wheels are misaligned, a driver will correct the bias with the steering.

All input information is formalized by defining a vector of quantities/numbers. This vector is known as the state and is chosen from a set called the state-space, $.

Policy

Since a state is used as input information to make a decision, we need a way to map states to actions. This map is called the policy and denoted by (“pi” - the ‘p’ in Greek). One often writes:

to denote that is a function that takes an element (state or state-vector) of the state-space and maps it to one element (action) of the action-space.

You’ll also see: which is to be read as “the action a taken by given the state s as the input”. This is also written as (note the different arrow with a vertical bar on the left).

Frequency of decision-making

Decisions are made across 1-dimensional time. In RL, continuous time is approximated by discretization i.e. time is assumed to tick at a constant clock-rate. For computers, this maps well since there’s an underlying clock that defines discrete time. Concretely, time is just a sequence .

Decision Process

We can put this all together to define the following decision-making process:

  • Start with initial state (observe the surroundings).

  • Use a given policy to make a decision: . [Caveat below]

  • Taking an action will change the state. In the car driving example, if the state is what you see and the action is “turn left by 10 degrees”, what you see will change after the action is taken. The new state is .

  • Use the policy to make the next decision: .

  • Continue this loop till some stopping criterion (destination reached).

The two new ingredients in the decision-making process (“decision process” for short) are the change in state after an action and the stopping criterion.

State changes

In any circumstance, performing an action will change the state. In general, this is a probabilistic change. In the car driving example, while our action will change what we see, so will the actions of other drivers. Even if we were to start at the same state (stopped at a red light at an intersection with no visible cars) and were to take the same action (press throttle at 50%), we’ll generally land in different new states depending on other cars that show up on the road.

The change in state is formalized by a new quantity called the transition probability or transition function denoted by:

or sometimes as:

This is to be read as “the probability of state at time t+1, given the state at time t, and action taken at time t, ” or “the probability of next state given current state and current action .

The transition function computes the probability of every new state . The actual new state is sampled from this function. This function is generally not known in advance. It is a property of the circumstance/environment one is in and in the car driving case, subsume all laws of physics, rules of the road, behaviors of other drivers etc.

There is a crucial assumption in defining the transition function this way. We wrote:

and not

or

for some k e.g. k = 5.

The probability of picking a new state only depends on the current state () and the current action (). The history of how one got to doesn’t matter and the past actions don’t matter. This is a simplifying assumption and is known as the Markov property. In practice, it is hard to establish if a decision process is truly Markovian. As we’ll see (in the Atari paper), one might have to extend the definition of state to make a process Markovian. Usually, one starts with a state definition and “bad performance” indicates that the state definition might be insufficiently informative which leads to adding more features.

Stopping criterion

Eventually, we want to stop the loop of state-action tuples. This is usually done in one of three ways:

  • A budget of how many steps to do this for.

  • No fixed budget - instead of runs till a goal is reached.

  • One can technically also run forever in an online manner.

Let’s recap the questions:

  • What do mean by “a given circumstance”? As an example, think of driving a car as the circumstance or task.

  • What is a decision? In the example, “braking”, “steering left by 10 degrees”, “steering right by 10 degrees”, “accelerator at 50%” could be some decisions.

  • How frequently do decision need to be made? One decision every 1 second would be too infrequent since a car at 60mph (~100kph) travels ~28m (~90 feet) in that time.

  • Given a sequence of already picked decisions, how do we evaluate the quality of the sequence? Alternately, what makes us prefer one sequence of decisions over another sequence?

We have answered most of these questions.

  • By circumstance, we mean an environment which costs of a state-space , action-space , a transition function .

  • Decisions or actions are chosen from the action space . Their effects are encapsulated by the transition function.

  • Time is discrete and ticks at some regular frequency. For us, it’s just a natural number.

The last question hasn’t been answered yet. Consider two trajectories (sequences of alternating states and actions):

and

Note: (“tau”) is the Greek “t” (for trajectory).

The super-script indicates which trajectory we are talking about. Each trajectory starts in potentially a different state (). Once an action is taken, the environments transitions to a different state according to the transition function.

Do we prefer one trajectory over another? Concretely, if each trajectory described one car driving trip, should we pick one over the other?

This notion of preference is made concrete by defining a reward function.

Reward Function

Given any state and an action , the reward function is a number (any real number). So, we have a sequence of rewards for any trajectory e.g.  and so on for each consecutive state-action pair.

The reward for the full trajectory is defined to be a simple sum of rewards:

Notational note: is notational shortcut for the sum as goes from 0 to in steps of 1. can be or a fixed finite number or a varying finite number, as we discussed before.

Now, we have a clear way of ranking trajectories. We prefer trajectories with higher sum-of-rewards . Usually, instead of saying “sum-of-rewards”, one says just “reward” where it’s clear from context whether one is talking about or individual per-time-step rewards .

This definition has an interesting consequence. We don’t just care about maximizing rewards at individual time-steps. By maximizing , we are forced to consider all time-steps i.e. to look at long-term behavior. In the car driving example, the trajectory level reward can be the total time to go from point A (initial state) to point B (final state). It might be tempting to cut across a median to drive in a straight line and thus minimize time, but this short-term thinking might lead to (a) getting pulled over by cops, (b) the car getting stuck in grass, (c) damaging the car on uneven surfaces, all of which would lead to worse long-term consequences.

In the case where one has arbitrarily long trajectories (), there’s another wrinkle - the total reward series (sum of terms) might not converge.

For example,

The series converges to a finite value.

On the other hand,

This series diverges i.e. if you keep adding more terms, the answer gets larger in an unbounded way. This is the famous geometric series:

if and only if . For any other r, the left-hand side diverges.

To ensure is finite, one inserts a discount factor, (“gamma” - Greek ‘g’), which is a number between 0 and 1 (exclusive of end-points) or formally to get:

Technical note: If is bounded (values lie between some min and max values), inserting ensures converges.

There’s a more “physical” interpretation of gamma. A reward of $100 today is preferrable to a reward of $100 in one year. A reward of $100 today could be invested in a risk-free asset (a savings account or 1-year treasury bills) at say 3% to get $103 in a year vs $100 a year later. In other words, a reward of $100 in one year is effectively $100/1.03 ~ 97 cents today (since if you invested this at 3%, you would get exactly $100 next year). is a reflection of this time-value of reward. would signify a 3% risk-free interest rate.

We now have a full formal setup. Reiterating,

  • By circumstance, we mean an environment which costs of a state-space , action-space , a transition function .

  • Decisions or actions are chosen from the action space . Their effects are encapsulated by the transition function.

  • Time is discrete and ticks at some regular frequency. For us, it’s just a natural number.

  • Trajectories are sequences of consecutive state-action tuples. For each (state, action) tuple (s,a), one can compute a reward . Sums of rewards (with potential discount factors) define a trajectory-level reward. Higher-reward trajectories are preferred. In reality, the definition of is up to us and the problem. Maximizing sum-of-rewards incentivizes long-term behavior.
